title: Asking for School Accommodations
summary: Navigate requesting academic support despite fear of seeming 'needy.' Practice preparing specific requests and choosing clarity over minimizing your needs.
author: HeyPsych Clinical Content Team
learningObjectives: Practice asking for accommodations despite fear of 'making a fuss'
Prepare 1-2 specific supports with real examples of impact
Interpret neutral responses from school staff as normal, not rejection
Close the loop with one clear next step

nodes.text:
Your school counselor offered to meet about accommodations for your anxiety. The appointment is in 20 minutes.

Your chest tightens at the thought. 'What if I'm just making a big deal out of nothing? Other people manage fine. What if they think I'm lazy or just making excuses?'

What do you do?

You're standing outside the counselor's office. Through the door, you can hear them wrapping up with another student.

Your mind races: 'I don't even know what to ask for. Maybe I should just deal with it on my own. Everyone else seems fine.'

The other student walks out, nodding politely as they pass you.

What do you do?

You tell yourself you'll reschedule for 'when you're more ready.' Maybe after you figure out exactly what you need. Maybe when you feel less anxious about asking.

But as days pass, nothing changes. The test anxiety, the presentation dread, the overwhelming pressure—all still there.

Postponing felt safer. But it didn't solve anything.

A week later, a new opportunity appears: the counselor sends a reminder email asking if you'd still like to meet.

You convince yourself you don't really need help. 'I can just try harder. Push through. It's not that bad.'

The relief is instant. But the anxiety during tests, the panic before presentations, the constant overwhelm—none of that goes away.

A few days later, you bomb a test you knew the material for. The anxiety froze you. Maybe you do need help after all.

You pull out your phone and quickly type:

'Extra time on tests—I freeze up and need time to refocus.'
'Quiet space for exams—crowded rooms make my anxiety worse.'

Having it written down makes it feel more real. More legitimate.

You take a breath and knock.

The counselor looks up with a warm smile. 'Hi! Come in. What can I help you with today?'

What do you say?

You step inside without a plan. The counselor looks up.

'Hi! Come in. What can I help you with today?'

Your mind blanks. You know you're struggling, but the words won't come together. What exactly do you need? How do you even explain it?

What do you say?

You ask for what you need. The counselor listens, taking notes, and responds:

'Okay, those are reasonable requests. A lot of students benefit from test accommodations. Let me explain the process...'

Their tone is neutral—professional, matter-of-fact. Not overly warm, not cold. Just... normal.

Your anxiety whispers: 'They think I'm weak. They're just being polite. I shouldn't have asked.'

But their words say otherwise.

What do you do?

You start with: 'I'm so sorry to take up your time, I know you're really busy and this probably isn't a big deal, but I've been having some trouble and I don't want to be dramatic but...'

The counselor interrupts gently: 'You're not taking up my time. This is exactly what I'm here for. What's going on?'

You manage to explain. The apologies came from a place of not wanting to be a burden—a feeling many people share when asking for help.

They outline the accommodation process. It helps, even if part of you still wonders if your needs are 'big enough' to deserve support. (They are.)

You say: 'I've just been really stressed and school has been hard lately...'

The counselor nods. 'I understand. Can you tell me more about what's been hardest? That'll help me figure out what support might help.'

It's hard to pinpoint specifics on the spot. Without preparation, the conversation feels scattered—not because you did anything wrong, but because putting struggles into words is genuinely difficult.

You leave wishing you'd had more to say. That's okay—it's information for next time.

Before leaving, you ask: 'What happens next? What do I need to do?'

The counselor gives you a clear plan: 'I'll draft a letter to your teachers outlining these accommodations. You'll need to bring this form to your doctor to fill out. Once I have that back, the accommodations will go into effect.'

You nod. You have a roadmap now.

You leave the office. The anxiety is still there, but quieter. You asked for help, you got a plan, and you know the next step.

Clarity beats confidence.

They finish explaining the process. You nod, say 'Thanks,' and head out.

As you walk away, you realize: you're not totally sure what to do next. Do you need paperwork? Do your teachers get notified automatically? When does this actually start?

You showed up and asked—that's real progress. The next step is just getting clarity on what comes next.

Their tone was neutral. But your mind insists: 'They think I'm overreacting. They're just being nice. I shouldn't have asked.'

You thank them quickly and leave. The conversation helped a little, but the mind-reading pulled you out of the moment.

You tried. But interpreting neutral as negative kept you from fully engaging.

endings.title: Confident Step
endings.text:
You did the hard thing. You met with the counselor, asked for specific accommodations with real examples, and—critically—closed the loop by asking what happens next.

Clarity beats confidence. You didn't need to feel perfectly sure of yourself. You just needed to show up, ask directly, and get specific.

This is what asking for accommodations looks like when you do it well: uncomfortable, brief, effective.

Next time will still be hard. But you know the formula now.

endings.title: Mixed But Moving
endings.text:
You went. That's more than avoiding. You showed up, asked for something, and got some help—even if you over-apologized, left without asking what's next, or let mind-reading pull you out of the moment.

You're building the skill. It's messy. That's normal.

Next time, try one thing: ask for the clear next step before you leave. 'What happens next? What do I need to bring?' That's the difference between partial help and real progress.

endings.title: Avoidance Loop
endings.text:
You chose comfort over asking for support. Maybe you postponed, or skipped entirely, or bailed at the door.

Avoidance feels like relief—until you're still struggling in tests, still panicking before presentations, still managing alone.

Accommodations aren't about being 'needy.' They're about getting support that helps you show what you actually know. And the only way to get that support is to ask.

Next time, try this: write down two specific accommodations, walk to the office, and ask for them. That's the whole rep.
